The proof encodes a max-cut instance directly into the three rankings, so a hard instance is literally a graph in disguise, and solving it exactly recovers a maximum cut. The mechanic: the visitor sees three rankings of a small set of items (six to ten) and drags the items into their own proposed aggregate order. A live counter shows total Kendall-tau distance to the three inputs while dragging, and on release the site reveals the true minimum, computed exactly offline from the max-cut graph the puzzle was built from. Turn one ships exactly that loop: one generated instance, the drag-to-rank interface, the live disagreement counter, and the reveal, with no explanation of max-cut needed yet. The hard part is making the hardness legible without a graph-theory lecture: a puzzle's difficulty should visibly correlate with something the visitor can see, such as how tangled the three inputs look, rather than being asserted. A later turn can add a difficulty dial tied to the underlying graph's edge count. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer conventions (as with erdos/) for the interface and workers/scores for a record table of fastest correct solves per difficulty tier, since checking a submitted aggregate against the true optimum is cheap and exact at this size.
mechanism: drag-sort a proposed compromise ranking against three fixed rankings and check it against the true minimum-disagreement aggregate
text: drag items to create a compromise between three rankings. live meter shows disagreement. release to see the best arrangement—which stays hard to find even when all three rankings nearly agree

paperTitle: Tampered Memory Elephant Random Walk on One-Dimensional Integer Lattice
name: half-memory
plan: The elephant random walk repeats, with fixed probability p, a uniformly-chosen step from its own past; above a threshold on p it turns superdiffusive. This paper asks how much of that memory can be corrupted before the effect disappears: split the timeline into a tampered set (steps replaced by fresh independent coin flips) and a retained set (ordinary elephant memory), and ask how large the retained fraction needs to be. The answer is a clean threshold at one half: if the retained fraction of steps stays above 1/2, the full diffusive/critical/superdiffusive phase transition in p survives; below 1/2, the walk is always merely diffusive no matter how strong p is; exactly 1/2 is its own boundary case. The mechanic: two sliders, memory strength p and retained fraction, and a canvas showing a walk (or a fan of several, for a cleaner signal) stepping in real time, plus a running estimate of its growth exponent from spread versus step count. Turn one ships the sliders, the animated walk, and the live exponent readout, with p defaulted into the superdiffusive range so dragging retained-fraction below one half is visibly a collapse back to plain diffusion. The hard part is getting a readable exponent out of a noisy finite simulation fast enough to feel responsive, likely by running several parallel walks and averaging mean-squared displacement rather than trusting one trajectory. The paper settles the deterministic-partition case and only conjectures the random one; a later turn can let visitors submit their own tampering patterns and the site tallies estimated exponents near the threshold as informal crowd evidence toward the open case. Reuse the math wing's explainer conventions and workers/scores for a submitted-pattern record table.
mechanism: dial a random walk's memory strength and how much of its memory survives tampering, then watch its growth exponent flip across a one-half threshold
text: dial a random walk's memory strength and corruption. watch it spread on a canvas. exactly at one half remaining, the spreading changes. below that threshold, stays the same regardless of memory strength

paperTitle: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
name: peek-or-poke
plan: People sometimes learn by watching someone else and sometimes by trying things themselves, and this paper models the choice as a cost-benefit calculation that requires theory of mind: an agent estimates how informative watching a specific other agent's next move would be, by reasoning about that agent's goal, and weighs it against the cost of learning directly. Validated on a game the authors built where players repeatedly choose to observe another agent or explore on their own, the 'Rational Mentalizing' model quantitatively matches real human choices. The mechanic reproduces that game: each round, the visitor sees a hidden-reward environment and a bot with a legible but not fully obvious goal, and chooses to peek (watch what the bot does next, learning something about the environment for free) or poke (spend the round exploring directly). Turn one ships one environment, one bot, the peek/poke choice, and a running tally of choices and outcomes, with no model comparison yet. A second turn overlays the Rational Mentalizing model's predicted peek/poke curve against the visitor's actual choices, so they can see where they over- or under-used social learning relative to the model. The hard part is tuning the bot's legibility: too obvious and peeking is free, trivializing the choice; too unreadable and peeking teaches nothing, and the mechanism the paper is about disappears. Reuse games/'s room machinery for pairing visitors with live or replayed bot runs, human/'s arcade-of-user-error framing for tone, and scores for personal history; since a thousand people playing this produces a live, larger-scale replication of the paper's own study, that aggregate is the crowd payoff, not a leaderboard.
mechanism: each round, choose to watch a bot's next move or explore the environment yourself, then compare your choices to a theory-of-mind utility model
text: each round peek (watch a bot's move) or poke (explore). the bot's trying to solve something partly visible. your pattern of choices should match how someone reasoning about the bot's goal would choose

paperTitle: Anonymous sharing is pairwise phase-blind
name: checkpoint-storm
plan: Checkpoint storms, synchronized bursts when many training jobs write to the same shared storage, are usually blamed on phase-locking, the same oscillator-coupling math that explains synchronized fireflies. This paper shows that blame is backwards for the ordinary case: model each job's write cycle as an oscillator coupled only through a shared resource that is anonymous, meaning the rate it hands an active job depends on how many jobs are active and not on which one, and the coupling vanishes exactly. For identical jobs the two-job phase-gap return map is the identity function, no attraction and no repulsion, and the firing order freezes forever, for any fleet size and any bandwidth cap; only a weak third-order effect survives, and it is a fixed point with more expanding directions than contracting ones, not something trajectories drift toward. Real synchrony only reappears once jobs stop being identical and interchangeable under a hard cap. The mechanic: a ring of animated jobs sharing one pipe, with two dials, anonymity (does the pipe treat jobs by identity or just by count) and heterogeneity (identical jobs or varied write/compute ratios), and a stated goal: make the write pulses lock into a storm. Turn one ships the ring, the two dials, and a live phase-gap-variance readout, with no scoring, just the challenge of watching it refuse to lock under full anonymity no matter how it is perturbed. The hard part is making a null result feel like a result: showing that different random starts drift apart rather than converge, unlike a firefly simulation, so the absence of synchrony reads as a finding rather than a bug. No existing surface's code applies directly; reuse packages/dataviz for the phase-gap chart.
mechanism: dial a shared resource's anonymity and a job fleet's heterogeneity, then try to force periodic write cycles into a synchronized storm
text: arrange jobs in a ring, all writing to a shared pipe. dial whether the pipe treats them anonymously and whether the jobs are identical. try to force their writes into a synchronized storm. but when the pipe is truly anonymous, it refuses to lock—no matter what

paperTitle: Quantum Chaos and Diffusive Transport from Geometric Randomness
name: corridor-width
plan: Quantum chaos usually needs either many interacting particles or disorder scattered into an otherwise regular lattice. This paper gets it from neither: non-interacting particles on a graph built from pure geometric randomness, layers of sites wired to the next layer with uniform-strength links but wired irregularly, go chaotic or not depending only on how wide the layers are. Wide layers push the system into full quantum chaos: energy levels show Wigner-Dyson repulsion and a particle placed on one site diffuses outward through the graph. Narrow, quasi-one-dimensional layers instead produce a spectrum where localized and delocalized states coexist, level repulsion is suppressed even as the delocalized states still carry a particle ballistically across the graph. No impurities were added anywhere; the wiring itself is the only randomness. The mechanic: a slider sets the corridor's layer width, regenerating a small randomly wired layered graph drawn as a branching maze; the visitor drops a particle on a node and watches it spread. Turn one ships the width slider, the graph generator, and the spreading animation using a simple discrete quantum-walk update, with no spectral statistics yet. A second turn adds a live level-spacing histogram beside the animation so the visitor can see repulsion versus clustering track the same slider that changes how the particle spreads. The hard part is doing real spectral statistics, diagonalizing the graph's Hamiltonian and binning the spacings, fast enough in-browser; capping the graph at a few hundred sites and precomputing a small library of graphs per width is more realistic than live diagonalization on every drag. Reuse packages/dataviz for the histogram; no existing surface's code applies directly, though the corridor-as-maze visual would sit comfortably beside the O'Neill pack's structural aesthetic if themed later.
mechanism: set a randomly wired graph's layer width and watch a quantum particle's spreading and its energy-level statistics flip between chaotic and localized
text: adjust a slider to build a wired corridor, then drop a quantum particle on it. watch whether it spreads or gets trapped as you adjust. the width alone decides—no impurities, no randomness, just geometry

paperTitle: Hash Chemistry: Minimal Models for Evolutionary Growth of Complexity
name: cardinality-leap
plan: Hash Chemistry scores entities of arbitrary size with a single deterministic hash function, which turns a modest rule into access to a combinatorially vast possibility space the paper calls a cardinality leap. The newest variant, Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry, adds spatial locality to how replicators compete, and run at large scale on a GPU the paper finds something specific: the size of the space itself acts as a control parameter. Below a threshold, populations stay compact and diverse; above it, growth tips into a runaway size-dominance regime where one lineage's descendants crowd out everything else, through a stochastic, nucleation-like transition. The mechanic: entities are short symbol strings, scored purely by hashing their contents, no training, no lookup table, so any child can invent a genuinely new structure. The visitor sets one dial, the size of the space, then runs generations of mutation and selection and watches whether the population stays compact or tips into one dominant giant. Turn one: a small non-spatial version — hash-scoring, mutation, selection, the size dial, and a live chart of entity-size distribution across generations, ending each run labelled compact or runaway. The hard part is that the transition is genuinely stochastic near the threshold: one run at a borderline size can go either way, so a single visitor watching once will see noise, not a phase transition. The fix is to aggregate: show a live histogram of how every visitor's run at each size setting resolved, so the actual phase boundary emerges from traffic rather than any one run. Reuse fluoddity's deterministic genome-scoring pattern, reef's crowd-aggregation habits, and packages/dataviz for the histogram.
mechanism: grid-size dial driving a hash-scored replicator population toward compact growth or runaway size-dominance
text: set how much space symbolic strings have and watch them either branch into diversity or crash into one dominant giant at a sharp threshold

paperTitle: Sumsets and generalized arithmetic progressions in multiplicative subgroups
name: sumcap
plan: The paper studies multiplicative subgroups A of a finite field's unit group and proves, among other things, that once A is not tiny and not nearly the whole group, no target value has an outsized number of representations as a sum of two elements of A — specifically, for index at least 3 and |A| at least 5, every nonzero c is hit by fewer than |A|/2 pairs. Restrict the toy to prime fields, where the subgroups are exactly the d-th power residues (quadratic residues, cubic residues, and so on), so a visitor's intuition about residues carries over cleanly. Pick a prime p and a divisor d of p−1; the app derives A automatically as the unique subgroup of that order, then computes r(c), the count of pairs (a,b) in A×A with a+b ≡ c mod p, for every c, and draws it as a bar around a ring of residues with the |A|/2 ceiling marked as a line. The hunt is for the c that comes closest to that ceiling — a claim anyone can check in one click by recomputing the pair (p, d, c). Turn one: a curated list of primes, a subgroup-order slider restricted to the theorem's valid regime, and the histogram with its ceiling line. The hard part is honesty at the edges: subgroups with |A| at most 4, or index below 3, sit outside the theorem's guarantee and can look deceptively similar on the same chart, so the UI must gray those settings out rather than silently plotting a bound that does not apply there. Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer convention (erdos, kakeya, capset) and workers/scores for a recomputable record table of closest approaches to the ceiling.
mechanism: pick a prime and subgroup order, then hunt the sumset histogram for its closest approach to the paper's density ceiling
text: pick a prime and subgroup order, then hunt the ring of sums for the outlier that comes closest to the paper's density bound

paperTitle: Synchronization, Kinematic Waves and Spike-Phase-Separation in Feedback Ising Neural Networks on Heterogeneous Graphs
name: kinwave
plan: The paper models neurons as a kinetic Ising network with a homeostatic feedback loop between excitability and population firing rate, and shows analytically how heterogeneity in the network's connectivity controls what the population does collectively. At low heterogeneity, the population settles into a synchronized limit cycle, born from an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation, everyone pulsing together. Raise the heterogeneity and, before synchronization takes hold each cycle, a kinematic wave sweeps visibly from low-degree periphery neurons inward to the high-degree hubs. Push heterogeneity further still and the whole thing freezes into a phase-separated state via a pitchfork bifurcation: some neurons locked high, others locked low, the collective rhythm gone for good. The mechanic is one dial, network heterogeneity, turning a small node-link graph from breathing in unison, to rippling from edge to center, to frozen and split. Turn one: implement the mean-field homeostatic update on a small synthetic network whose degree spread is set by the one heterogeneity parameter, animate node colour by firing state, and plot the population firing rate live alongside it, so the sync-to-frozen transition reads as a trace collapsing, not just as nodes going still. The hard part is that the frozen state can look like the sim merely stalling unless the trace shows the specific signature the paper reports: the per-neuron rate and the per-synapse rate pulling apart from each other as heterogeneity rises, which needs its own small chart to be legible at all. Reuse neuro, the wing built for cognitive-science models reimplemented from their papers and shown against the published result, where the homeostasis piece already lives, and packages/dataviz for the rate traces.
mechanism: one heterogeneity dial driving a feedback neuron network between synchronized pulsing, a periphery-to-hub wave, and a frozen split
text: turn the heterogeneity dial: watch neurons pulse together, then ripple from edges inward, then lock into a frozen split

paperTitle: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
name: recourse-gap
plan: Algorithmic recourse tells a rejected applicant what to change to get approved, but the paper shows most such advice only cares about flipping the model's output, not whether the change reflects real improvement versus gaming the surface features. Its causal performative framework routes a recourse action through a small causal graph connecting observed features to the true, hidden qualification, and shows that policies ignoring that structure induce large behavioral responses that degrade once the model retrains on them, while causal-aware recourse settles into stable equilibria that resist gaming. The mechanic: a visitor plays a rejected applicant against a shared classifier and is offered two possible actions, one a cosmetic feature flip, one a change that actually runs through the hidden causal path to the true qualification, without being told which is which. They act, see the decision move, and can press a shared retrain button that folds the whole population's recent actions back into the classifier. The gaming action's success rate visibly decays after each retrain; the causal one keeps working, because it moved the thing the label actually depends on. Turn one: one small causal graph, two candidate actions, a single applicant's decision, and a retrain button whose effect on the two actions' success rates is shown as a running pair of numbers. The hard part is pacing: the lesson only lands if retrains are frequent enough that the decay of the gaming action reads as a pattern within a few clicks, not as one ambiguous random fluctuation. Reuse human, the arcade of user error, whose whole premise is a person mishandling a system, and workers/scores for population-level gaming-survives-N-retrains tracking.
mechanism: choose a recourse action against a shared classifier that periodically retrains on the crowd's behavior
text: play a rejected applicant choosing between cosmetic and causal recourse actions, then watch which one keeps working as the shared classifier retrains

paperTitle: Eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations of rational numbers via optimal control
name: sylvester
plan:
An Egyptian fraction writes a number as a sum of distinct unit fractions: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/11, say. The greedy algorithm builds one for any target by always subtracting the largest unit fraction that still fits underneath it. The paper answers a question going back to Erdos and Graham: is greedy eventually the best way to underapproximate — the k-term sum closest to the target from below — or can a smarter choice of denominators always beat it? For every positive rational, greedy wins forever after some finite number of terms, in both the version where denominators may repeat and the version where they must stay distinct. It also builds an irrational number where greedy is optimal and unique at every single step, with no catching-up needed.

The mechanic: pick a target rational, and watch two term-by-term expansions build underneath it on a number line — greedy on top, the true best k-term underapproximation (found by search) below. For most fractions the two rows agree almost immediately; the site marks the term index where they lock together for good. Turn one ships that single race for one hand-picked fraction with a visible crossover marker, no leaderboard yet.

The hard part: computing the true best k-term underapproximation is a search over which denominators to use, not a formula, and it gets expensive fast — the toy needs a term cap (maybe 6) and a fraction picker that stays inside what a browser can brute-force in the time a visitor will wait.

Reuse the math wing's single-file explainer pattern and the number-line device from the Erdos rectangle toy, and scores for a record table once a search-your-own-fraction hunt ships: crowd value is finding rationals where greedy takes unusually long to catch up, verifiable by anyone re-running the same two rows.
mechanism: race the greedy Egyptian-fraction algorithm against the true best underapproximation and find where they merge
text: watch two methods build fractions underneath your target and race to merge: one always grabs the biggest unit fraction that fits, the other searches for the true best. they always converge, but the gap between them before they lock is where the story lives

paperTitle: Convergence to the exact kinetics of the one-dimensional Riviera model
name: riviera
plan:
The Riviera model is random sequential deposition on a 1D lattice with one extra rule: you can build on an empty lot unless doing so would leave a single vacant lot pinned between two houses on both sides — that lot becomes permanently unbuildable, an isolated gap. Building continues at uniformly random empty lots until every remaining empty lot is one of these stranded singles: the street is jammed. No exact formula for the final fraction of lots built, the jamming density, is known; the paper derives an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations for the process and shows a systematic closure at increasing order converges very fast toward the true value, without ever writing that value down in closed form.

The toy: a street of lots, click (or auto-run) to attempt a build at a random empty lot; lots that fill turn built, lots that become permanently isolated turn red, and the run ends when nothing empty remains except stranded ones. Turn one ships one street, one run, and the final density displayed at the end — a single number, no history yet.

The mechanic gets its stakes from what nobody has: the exact jamming density. Because the paper never gives a closed form, the honest crowd move is aggregation — every visitor's run is one more independent sample, and the site keeps a running mean across every completed street, shown converging toward the paper's own high-order numerical estimate as runs accumulate. That's the hard part to get right: the running average has to read as approaching a number nobody can currently write down exactly, not as a personal high score, or the game is pointless after the first jam.

Reuse scores for the aggregate counter (sum of density times runs, not a personal leaderboard) and a plain canvas strip — no build, no worker changes beyond that.
mechanism: randomly build houses along a street under one rule and watch the block jam
text: click empty lots to randomly build houses until the street jams. the exact jamming density has no formula—the only way to pin it down is running a thousand simulations and averaging the results. each of your runs adds one more point to the crowd's estimate

paperTitle: Evolutionary adaptation through bet-hedging in finite populations under fluctuating environments
name: hedge
plan:
A minimal birth-death model: individuals inherit a phenotypic strategy — how spread-out their offspring's phenotypes are across a randomly switching environment. Pure bet-hedging survives crashes but grows slowly; pure specialism grows fast in one environment and can be wiped out when it switches. The paper's finding is that population size decides which strategy evolution actually converges to: large populations settle on the growth-maximizing strategy because they can absorb an occasional bad generation, while small populations evolve toward the more risk-averse, extinction-resistant strategy instead, facing the identical fluctuating environment. It gives a heuristic approximation for where that split falls.

The toy: two colonies, same environment-switching schedule, different starting sizes, run side by side across many generations. Each colony's evolved bet-hedging parameter is plotted live, and, periodically, the shared environment flips. The payoff moment is a flip that would wipe out a non-hedging population — the large colony has often drifted less cautious and takes a real hit, while the small one, having evolved more spread, rides it out. Turn one ships exactly that: two colonies, one slider for switching rate, a run button, and the two evolved-strategy traces.

What's hard: the model is stochastic and the interesting behavior, a visible near-extinction in the large colony, needs enough generations and the right switching rate to show up in a single run without a long wait — probably pre-tuned defaults rather than exposing every parameter from day one, or most runs will be visually uneventful.

The crowd angle: let visitors submit switching-rate and population-size pairs and log which colonies went extinct, building a shared map of the danger zone rather than each visitor discovering it alone. Reuse scores for that log; no other surface needed.
mechanism: run two populations of different size through the same random environment switches and see which strategy evolution favors
text: run two colonies through the same random environmental switches, one large and one small. evolution shapes each into a different strategy: the big one can afford specialists, the small one spreads its bets as insurance. watch them diverge as the world flips around them

paperTitle: Mpemba effect in a chemomechanical model of the Kinesin molecular motor
name: mpemba
plan:
The Mpemba effect is the famous claim that a system started farther from equilibrium can relax faster than one started closer, usually discussed for water and freezing. This paper finds it in a specific biological system: a six-state chemomechanical network model of the Kinesin motor protein, the one that walks along microtubules by cycling through ATP-binding states. Two different starting distributions over those six states, one nominally closer to equilibrium, race toward it — and the paper shows the farther one can win, both when the motor sits at rest and when it is being chemically or mechanically driven, mapping which regions of a two-parameter phase diagram produce the inversion versus the boring, expected outcome. It also finds the effect shows up in something you could measure on a real motor: the relaxation of its stepping velocity, not just its internal state probabilities.

The toy: two colored tokens, each a different starting distribution over the six kinesin states, dropped onto a shared free-energy landscape and left to relax; a small readout tracks each one's distance from equilibrium over time. Most starting pairs behave as expected — closer wins. Turn one ships that single race for one pre-set pair, with the states and landscape drawn plainly enough to read as a real molecular machine, not an abstract Markov chain.

The hard part: finding a starting pair that actually inverts is a search over the paper's two-parameter phase diagram, so the toy needs that diagram as a background layer visitors can click into, not a blind random-pair generator that mostly produces uninteresting races.

Reuse scores once the phase diagram ships: a record for the largest confirmed inversion (biggest head start, still loses) found, verifiable by anyone rerunning that exact pair.
mechanism: pick two starting distances from equilibrium for a molecular motor and race them to see which settles first
text: drop two starting points for a molecular motor onto its energy map and watch them both relax toward equilibrium. the point closer to rest usually reaches it first, but sometimes the farther point gets there faster. that flip is what the paper proves can happen

paperTitle: A data-driven stage-structured host-parasitoid model for optimizing Trichogramma interventions against soybean pod borer (Leguminivora glycinivorella) outbreaks
name: trichogramma
plan:
A calibrated model of a real pest problem: the soybean pod borer, and the tiny parasitic wasp (Trichogramma) farmers release as its egg-killing predator. The model couples the pest's full life stages to the wasp's egg-parasitism and was fit to field data from Jilin province by MCMC. From it the paper derives an economic injury level — 0.0389 larvae per square meter, the density above which crop damage costs more than acting would — and finds two answers for how to intervene: a continuous release rate of 2.645 wasps per unit time holds the pest below that line without wasting parasitoids on an already-suppressed population, and if you release in batches instead, every 5 days is the balance between suppression and how often a farm can realistically act.

The toy hands you the release schedule instead of the paper's optimizer: pick a strategy — steady rate, or batches on an interval you choose — run a season against the coupled pest-wasp dynamics, and get scored on two numbers, days spent over the injury threshold and total wasps spent. The paper's own optimum, 2.645 continuous or every 5 days, is shown as a reference line on the scoreboard, not the answer key — visitors are free to try uneven schedules or front-loaded releases the paper's fixed-strategy analysis never tried.

Turn one: the coupled dynamics running for one fixed schedule (the paper's continuous rate) with the two gauges, injury-threshold line and wasp count, visible across a season, no schedule editor yet.

Hard part: the underlying model is stage-structured on both species — the toy needs to run that faithfully enough that beating 2.645 means something, not a cartoon simplification that makes every strategy look equally good.
